# The CPU waits for memory {style="text-align: center;"}

## The memory hierarchy

- Add two floats: **< 1 ns**. Fetch from RAM: **~100 ns**.

. . .

| Level | Size | Latency | If L1 = 1 s |
|---|---|---|---|
| registers | ~100s B | ~0 | instant |
| **L1** | 32–64 KB / core | ~1 ns | 1 s |
| **L2** | 256 KB–1 MB | ~4 ns | 4 s |
| **L3** | 8–32 MB | ~15 ns | 15 s |
| **RAM** | 16–64 GB | ~100 ns | **~2 min** |

::: {.notes}
While waiting, the core could have done hundreds of operations.
This machine: L1d 544 KiB total (14 instances), L2 18 MiB total (9 × 2 MiB instances, not one core's cache), L3 24 MiB
shared. Hybrid CPU (P/E/LP-E cores) — per-core L1 differs, hence "instances".
`lscpu` shows it; the script asks students to compare with their own.
:::

## Caches rely on locality

- **Temporal**: used now → used again soon.
- **Spatial**: used now → **neighbors** next.
- Memory moves in **lines** of 64 B = 8 Float64.


## Same array, growing size {style="text-align: center;"}

. . .

Sum the **same array** many times, from **8 KB to 64 MB**.

. . .

L1 ≈ 1 ns, RAM ≈ 100 ns.

. . .

> ### How much slower per access at 64 MB?

. . .

> *(~100×? Write it down.)*

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "1. The memory hierarchy — the cache cliff"

## The cache cliff, measured

. . .

```julia
for _ in 1:passes                 # repeated_sum(a, passes)
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(a)
        s += a[i]
    end
end
```

. . .

| footprint | ns / access | lives in |
|---|---|---|
| 8 KB | **0.049** | L1 |
| 4 MB | **0.128** | L2 / L3 |
| 64 MB | **0.317** | RAM (> 24 MiB L3) |

. . .

> Steps visible. But [**6.5×, not ~100×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. Why?

::: {.notes}
Absolute values are machine- and load-sensitive: run at rest and look for the
JUMPS, not the exact ns. Full sweep (8 KB → 64 MB) is in the notebook/script: show one table,
not the whole sweep.
:::

## Why 6.5×? Throughput vs latency {#latency}

- **Latency**: the wait for **one unpredictable** access (the table).
- Our loop reads **in order** → hardware loads the next lines early.
- We pay for the **bandwidth** (throughput), not for each wait.

. . .

> 100× is real when the next address is [**unpredictable**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (linked list, random indices).

::: {.notes}
Not "the table is wrong" nor "machine noise". The part of the hardware that
loads lines early is the *prefetcher*. Latency and bandwidth are different
resources; a streaming sum is bandwidth-bound, a linked-list walk is latency-bound.
The same pair comes back with batching: time per request vs examples per second.
:::

# Experiment 1 — locality {style="text-align: center;"}

## Two walks, same maths

. . .

Sum an 8000×8000 matrix, two loop orders:

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
# COLUMN by column
for j in axes(M, 2)
    for i in axes(M, 1)
        s += M[i, j]
    end
end
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
# ROW by row
for i in axes(M, 1)
    for j in axes(M, 2)
        s += M[i, j]
    end
end
```
:::
::::

. . .

> **Which one is faster, and by how much?** ▶ Script: cell "2. Locality — the same sum, walked two ways"

## A4 — debrief: 11.9× for swapping two loops {#a4-debrief .smaller}

. . .

Julia, 8000² Float64 = 512 MB ≫ cache:

. . .

| walk | time | each 64 B line… |
|---|---|---|
| columns | **30.4 ms** | **fully used** (8 values) |
| rows | **361.4 ms** | **one** value, then evicted |

- Julia: **column by column**. NumPy default (C-contiguous): **row by row** — the opposite.

. . .

> **Rule:** inner loop along [**contiguous memory**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. Wrong order: silently slow.

::: {.notes}
Julia: M[i,j] and M[i+1,j] are neighbors; the Python track found the opposite ranking.
"Row-major" is the default for the C-contiguous arrays used here; a NumPy array can also be
F-contiguous or a strided view. The rule is about the layout you actually have, not the language.
:::

## Test the locality explanation 🔬

. . .

If Julia just "preferred columns", the gap would show at **any** size.

. . .

> ### Shrink the matrix. When does the gap vanish?

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Test the locality explanation"

## Test the locality explanation — debrief

. . .

| size | footprint | rows / columns |
|---|---|---|
| 100² | 78 KB — **fits** in cache | **0.9×** |
| 4000² | 122 MB — **spills** | **7.2×** |

- The gap appears **when the data outgrows the cache**.

. . .

> The gap comes from [**whether the next value is already in cache**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

::: {.notes}
Small matrix: everything is already close, so the order cannot matter.
Strongest argument of the module: it supports a locality explanation; cache, prefetching and TLB
effects are not isolated — say "consistent with", not "proves". Pluto: interactive slider.
Script: full table (100² → 4000²).
:::

# Experiment 2 — batching {style="text-align: center;"}

## One example at a time, or a lot at once?

- `W * x`: each weight loaded, used **once**.
- `W * X`, **B** columns: each weight used **B times** per load.

. . .

```julia
y = W * x     # 1 example
Y = W * X     # B examples
```

. . .

> Same examples, same results. Batching [**reuses the data it loaded**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

::: {.notes}
Not a GPU trick: if the mechanism is reuse, it must already pay on the CPU.
:::

## Batching on the CPU

. . .

`W`: 4096² Float32 = **64 MiB** > L3. Same examples, one `W * x` each, or `W * X` by lots of `B`.

. . .

> ### What happens to the time **per example**?

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "3. Batching: one layer W, B examples"

## A5 — debrief: batching, measured on the CPU {#a5-debrief .smaller}

. . .

`W` = 64 MiB. One by one (`W * x`): **1090 µs / example**.

. . .

| B | total | µs / example | vs one by one |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.55 ms | 2551.8 | 0.4× |
| 8 | 5.65 ms | 706.0 | 1.5× |
| 64 | 11.06 ms | 172.9 | 6.3× |
| 256 | 39.06 ms | 152.6 | 7.1× |
| 1024 | 141.80 ms | 138.5 | [**7.9×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |

. . .

> **Compare** with your table (4 MiB `W`). Same gain? **Explain** why.

::: {.notes}
B=1 here is a one-column matrix product (W * X[:,1:1]), slower than a true matrix-vector
product (2.55 vs 1.09 ms): a lot of one is not the reference, and it is not free.
Against the B=1 row of this table the ratio would read 18.4×; against the honest one-by-one
reference it is 7.9×. Quote 7.9×.
Activity with a 4 MiB W: do NOT expect the gain to vanish. On a test machine (1 BLAS thread) it
was still ~9× at B=64: W no longer streams from RAM, but it does not fit in L1/L2 either, and
one call per example pays its own overhead. Several mechanisms, one ratio: the honest debrief
is "which measurement separates them?" — vary m, vary BLAS threads.
numpy (python/4) gives almost the same numbers as Julia on the 64 MiB case.
:::

## Why B = 1024 barely helps any more

. . .

2551.8 → 172.9 (B=64) → 152.6 (B=256) → 138.5 µs: **flattens**.

- `W` = **64 MiB** > **24 MiB L3**: a *fixed* RAM stream per lot.
- Batching divides it by B:

. . .

$$\text{time per example} \approx \text{compute} + \frac{\text{stream } W}{B}$$

- B ≈ 256: second term tiny.


::: {.notes}
The 1/B model fits: 138.5 µs ≈ pure compute per example; 2551.8 ≈ that plus the whole W stream.
This is why python/4 uses n=4096: at 2000² W (16 MB) fits in L3 and the
mechanism disappears.
:::

## A bigger batch is not always better

- **Throughput**: examples per second. Grows with `B`, then flattens.
- **Latency**: one request waits for the 63 others of its lot.

. . .

> Choose `B` for the **objective**: overnight job or interactive service?

::: {.notes}
Same pair as earlier today (one access vs a stream). Last question of the activity. For the project: state which of the two you optimize.
:::

## What we keep

:::{.nonincremental}
- **Neighbors** are cheap, **jumps** are not.
- Inner loop along contiguous memory: check **your** layout.
- Batching **reuses loaded data**, even on a CPU.
- Throughput and latency are **different objectives**.
:::

# Only if time {#appendix style="text-align: center;"}

## numpy hides the layout cost, doesn't remove it

. . .

C-order vs F-order arrays, 8000²:

. . .

| numpy | ratio | why |
|---|---|---|
| `A.sum(axis=0)` | **≈ 1×** | numpy **reorders** |
| copy F→C / C→C | **13.2×** (109.5 / 8.3 ms) | source/destination layouts differ |

. . .

> [numpy hides the layout cost; Julia shows it. Neither removes it.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

::: {.notes}
On `sum`, someone wrote the reordering for you. A mismatched copy or a
hand-written loop: the full penalty is back.
Measured: sum(axis=0) C/F = 1.14× at 8000², 0.77× at 2000² — noise around 1×,
and load-sensitive (0.45× seen under load). Don't over-read either side of 1×.
Demo lives in the Python notebook (python/4).
:::

## Allocating is memory traffic too

. . .

```julia
z = 2 .* x .+ y      # NEW 76 MiB array
z .= 2 .* x .+ y     # reuses z
```

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Optional — allocating is memory traffic too"

. . .

| n = 10⁷ | time | allocated |
|---|---|---|
| `z = …` | 54 ms | 76 MiB |
| `z .= …` | **17 ms** | [**0 bytes**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |

. . .

> One dot: **~3×**. But **measure**: the gain isn't always there.

::: {.notes}
A new array is fresh memory to fetch and fill.
Same for BLAS: `A * B` allocates, `mul!(C, A, B)` reuses C. At n = 2000 on this
laptop the gain swings from no gain to ~3× from run to run (hybrid cores):
measure. numpy gains only ~1.4× with `out=`: it can't FUSE `2*x + y` into one
pass. For matrix × VECTOR the output is tiny and the gain vanishes. Measured at rest: mul!(y, W, x) on matrix-VECTOR was actually SLOWER than W * x
(760 vs 468 µs). On the GPU, in place gains nothing in Julia either (2.10 vs
1.82 ms; CUDA.jl allocates from a pool) — whereas torch in place does gain
(1.35 → 0.80 ms). The law is "allocation = memory traffic".
:::

## Arithmetic intensity: FLOP per byte

. . .

| n×n, Float64 | FLOP | bytes | intensity |
|---|---|---|---|
| mat × **vec** | 2n² | 8n² | **0.25** — constant |
| mat × **mat** | 2n³ | ~24n² | **~n/12** — if each matrix crosses memory once |

- **Low**: compute waits for loads → **memory-bound**.
- **High**: reuse can shift the limit toward **compute**.

. . .

> To compare sizes, compare [**GFLOP/s**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, not seconds.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Optional — arithmetic intensity"

::: {.notes}
Work per byte loaded; a FLOP = one `+` or `*`.
Don't compare seconds: they do different work. GFLOP/s = 10⁹ FLOP per second.
The batching demo as throughput: 13.1 → 47.5 → 194.1 → 219.9 → 242.3 GFLOP/s for B = 1 … 1024.
Intensity is per BYTE, not per value (8× apart for Float64) — be consistent.
BLAS-3 (GEMM) tiling is what approaches reuse (ideal three-matrix Float64 traffic gives n/12 FLOP/byte): each tile is reused from cache.
:::
